title: Microsoft publishes MAI Code of Conduct — Nadella draws a line on superintelligence
subtitle: The rulebook governing Microsoft's first-party AI models goes to public consultation on September 14, with Satya Nadella backing 'deliberate pacing' and embedded evaluators.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Microsoft published a Code of Conduct for its first-party MAI models on September 14, 2026, opening it to public consultation. CEO Satya Nadella teased the rulebook the day before in a Saturday essay on X and wrote that Microsoft "welcomes the deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right." Nadella stated the guiding principle in one line: "Any pursuit of superintelligence has to be grounded in the core principle that if the AI we build is not helping humanity and under human control, it's not worth pursuing." The document lands the same weekend Anthropic's Dario Amodei called for a global AI slowdown and Sam Altman said OpenAI would not IPO in 2026.

The mechanics matter more than the mission statement. Microsoft's approach — broad access at every layer of the AI stack, enterprise control of learning loops, and an underlying Code of Conduct for first-party models — is what the company will hold itself to when its own MAI series ships. Nadella also endorsed "embedded evaluators" (independent inspection built into model deployments) and warned that alignment work "cannot be controlled by a handful of entities" and must draw from academia, other countries, and civil society. Public consultation, rather than a fait accompli release, is Microsoft's way of putting that plurality claim on the record.

In context: Microsoft is a rare position among the frontier labs — it ships MAI models of its own and is OpenAI's largest backer. A code of conduct signed by both parties would carry a lot more weight than one just written by Redmond. Whether OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind adopt or contest the document over the next 30 days will tell us whether "deliberate pacing" is an industry norm forming in real time or a Microsoft-flavored PR moment. The last time an industry code of conduct got this much attention was the 2023 White House voluntary commitments — worth reading Microsoft's draft side-by-side.

For learners: when a company publishes a rulebook for its own product, read who it binds. A code of conduct that only names things Microsoft was already going to do is marketing; one that names commitments a competitor could enforce is governance. The difference is usually in the paragraph nobody quotes.
